messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame, a 50-year-old plumber from an African background, had always prided himself on his ability to fix things — both in his work and in his life. However, ever since the night of the assault, everything changed. He had been returning home from a late job when he was confronted by a group of men in a dark alley. They demanded his wallet, and when he hesitated, they pushed him violently to the ground, kicking him repeatedly while he lay there helpless. The memory of that night haunted him relentlessly; he could still see the faces of his attackers, the cold gleam of a knife, and the sound of their laughter as they walked away, leaving him broken and battered. 

In the weeks that followed, Kwame found himself retreating into an increasingly narrow world. The once vibrant streets he had navigated with ease became sources of anxiety and dread. He could only feel safe in a limited number of familiar places, primarily his home, which now felt like a fortress. Each unexpected movement nearby — the rustle of leaves, a passing car — sent him into a state of panic, as if he were still under threat from his attackers. This constant state of hyper-vigilance was exhausting, leading to trouble falling asleep and staying asleep, his mind racing with intrusive memories that he could only visualize as fleeting images rather than articulate thoughts. The guilt he felt upon recalling the assault was overwhelming; he would replay the moment over and over, convinced that if he had acted differently, perhaps he could have avoided the attack altogether.

This sense of guilt intertwined with a growing belief that he was no longer the man he used to be. Kwame felt as if he had lost a part of himself, the confident and capable plumber who could tackle any challenge. Instead, he was plagued by self-doubt, questioning his ability to handle even the simplest tasks, both at work and in his personal life. He could no longer trust himself to make the right decisions, haunted by the notion that he could fail again. This self-appraisal deepened his feelings of vulnerability, intensifying his perception of threat in the world around him. He became convinced that he would never be able to return to his previous life, feeling that nothing had been done to address the injustice he experienced. 

The memories of that terrible night became a constant companion, feeding into his fears and anxieties. Each time he recalled the event, it felt as though he were reliving it all over again, the images striking him with a sense of danger that rendered him powerless. He avoided crowded places, no longer willing to risk encountering anything that might remind him of the assault. His relationships with his wife and friends strained under the weight of his withdrawal. The social outings they had once enjoyed together now felt like insurmountable challenges, as he feared he might break down or lash out if something triggered his memories.

As the months passed, Kwame's world shrank further, and he began to realize that he could no longer ignore the toll the trauma was taking on his life. The isolation, the guilt, the constant anxiety — they had become unbearable. He finally sought help, driven by a deep-seated hope that he might reclaim the life he once had. Yet, as he walked into the therapist's office, he couldn't shake the feeling that he might not be capable of facing the truths that lay ahead. What frightened him most was the fear that he would never be able to trust himself again, and that the man he used to be would remain forever lost in the shadows of that dark alley.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not illustrate how negative appraisals lead to a perceived threat in Kwame's experience.
The vignette fails to demonstrate how memories of the assault contribute to a sense of threat for Kwame.
The vignette does not connect the sense of threat Kwame feels to the memories of the assault, lacking a clear causal relationship.
